New Moon
NOO MOON
n. phrase
New + moon; Hebrew chōdesh (new moon, month) from chādash (to be new); the first day of each month in the Jewish lunar calendar, marked by special offerings and the cessation of business in OT Israel.

Biblical Definition

The new moon (Hebrew chōdesh, both new moon and month) was a recurring monthly observance in OT Israel—the first day of each lunar month, marked by special offerings (Num 28:11-15), the blowing of trumpets (Num 10:10), the cessation of business (Amos 8:5), and the gathering of family for the new-moon feast (1 Sam 20:5, 18, 24-29). The Jewish calendar being lunar, the new moon was a visible monthly event, observed when the first sliver of the new crescent appeared in the western sky after sunset. The biblical doctrine of the new moon has several structural dimensions. First, the worship-and-offering function: the new moon was a time of special sacrifice. Numbers 28:11-15 prescribes two young bullocks, one ram, seven lambs of the first year for a burnt offering, with their meal offerings and drink offerings, plus a kid for a sin offering, in addition to the daily continual burnt offering. Each new month opened with a renewed dedication to the LORD. Second, the calendrical function: the new moon set the date for the various monthly observances. The Passover, Day of Atonement, Feast of Tabernacles, and other annual feasts were all dated relative to particular new-moon dates. The new-moon observance therefore served the calendrical infrastructure on which the rest of the festal year depended. Third, the prophetic-and-pastoral use: the new moon, together with the Sabbaths, appears in the prophets as marking the structured worship-life of Israel, often in contexts that warn against empty observance divorced from heart-religion. Isaiah 1:13-14: bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth. The LORD does not condemn the new moon as such (He instituted it); He condemns its observance by a people whose hands were full of blood. Fourth, the eschatological-and-NT register: Colossians 2:16-17 treats new moons together with the OT feast-days and sabbaths as shadows whose substance is Christ: let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. The new-moon observance, like the other OT calendar items, is fulfilled and superseded in the New Covenant by the Christ to whom it pointed. The eschatological echo is in Isaiah 66:22-23: for as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the LORD, so shall your seed and your name remain. And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD. In the new heavens and new earth, the worship of God continues in a rhythm that echoes the OT new-moon-and-sabbath calendar, with all flesh gathered to worship Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NEW MOON as the moon in its first visible crescent after conjunction with the sun; in scripture, the first day of each Hebrew lunar month, marked by special offerings and trumpet-blowing in OT Israel; with the other OT calendar items, treated by Paul as a shadow whose substance is Christ (Col 2:16-17).

expand to see more

NEW MOON — The moon when it is in conjunction with the sun, and consequently invisible; or rather, the moon in its first visible crescent. Among the Jews, the first day of each lunar month, marked by special offerings (Num 28:11-15) and the blowing of trumpets (Num 10:10).

MOON, n. — The heavenly body which revolves round the earth, the second of the great lights of heaven (Gen 1:16); used in scripture for the marking of months and the festal calendar.

Key Scripture

Numbers 28:11 — "And in the beginnings of your months ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the LORD; two young bullocks, and one ram, seven lambs of the first year without spot."

Colossians 2:16-17 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Isaiah 1:13-14 — "Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth."

Isaiah 66:23 — "And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The new-moon observance is corrupted, on one side, by certain Hebrew-roots and Messianic movements that have urged Christian observance of the new-moon calendar as continuing covenantal obligation (against Col 2:16-17)—and on the other by the general loss of any sense of structured monthly worship-rhythm in much contemporary church life, leaving the calendar entirely shapeless beyond the weekly Lord’s Day.

expand to see more

The Hebrew-roots and certain Messianic movements have, in various forms, urged Christian observance of the new-moon calendar as continuing covenantal obligation: Christians should mark the new moons, observe the feasts of Israel, return to the OT calendar as the structure of Christian worship. Paul explicitly rebukes this kind of imposition in Colossians 2:16-17, treating new moons together with feasts and sabbaths as a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. The OT calendar was the shadow; Christ is the substance; the New Covenant believer is not bound to observe OT new moons, feasts, and sabbaths as continuing covenantal obligations. The recovery is the recovery of the substance over the shadow: every new moon, every feast, every Sabbath has been fulfilled in Christ, and the New Covenant believer finds the substantive worship-reality of all the OT calendar items in his union with Christ and his ordinary Lord’s Day gathering.

The opposite corruption is the general loss of any sense of structured worship-rhythm in much contemporary church life. The Christian week, month, and year have become largely shapeless in many traditions: the weekly Lord’s Day remains (often diminished), but the monthly and annual rhythms that Christian tradition (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed) has variously preserved—the seasons of Advent, Lent, Easter, Pentecost; the saints’ days; the special providences’ commemorations—have been largely abandoned. Some abandonment is salutary (the medieval calendar had accumulated much that was unsubstantial); some is loss (the structured worship-rhythm of the Christian year has substantive pastoral value when ordered around Christ’s person and work). The Christian liberty to structure the calendar is real (Rom 14:5-6; Col 2:16); but the absence of any structure is its own loss. Recover both ends. Refuse the Hebrew-roots imposition of OT calendar items as continuing obligation, and refuse the shapeless un-rhythmic worship-life that has lost the value of structured Christian time. The biblical pattern is liberty in the particulars under the rule of the body of Christ: weekly Lord’s Day non-negotiable, annual rhythms wisely ordered around the gospel’s great events, and the believer’s worship-life shaped by patterns that point to Christ as the substance of every shadow.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chōdesh (new moon, month), from chādash (to be new); the first day of each lunar month in OT Israel, marked by special offerings (Num 28:11-15) and trumpet-blowing (Num 10:10); treated by Paul as a shadow whose substance is Christ (Col 2:16-17); echoed in the eschatological new-moon-and-sabbath worship of the new heavens and earth (Isa 66:23).

expand to see more

Hebrew chōdesh (H2320) — new moon, month (276 OT uses; both senses).

Hebrew chādash (H2318) — to be new (the verb behind the noun).

Hebrew rō’sh chōdesh — head of the month (the Jewish term for the new-moon day).

Greek neomēnia (G3561) — new moon (Col 2:16, the only NT occurrence).

"From one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me—Isa 66:23’s eschatological echo of the new-moon-and-sabbath worship-rhythm in the new heavens and earth."

"The new moon in OT Israel marked the calendrical infrastructure on which the festal year depended, with special offerings and trumpet-blowing inaugurating each month."

"Hebrew-roots movements impose OT new-moon observance as continuing obligation against Col 2:16-17; the shapeless contemporary calendar loses all structured worship-rhythm; biblical pattern is Christian liberty with the gospel’s great events providing the substantive structure."
